lesson.title: What '95 Percent Confident' Actually Means (and What It Doesn't)
lesson.summary: A confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method used to build the interval, not the probability that one specific already-computed interval contains the true parameter.
lesson.body:
Once a confidence interval is computed, it is tempting to describe it loosely, but AP Statistics rewards, and real statistical reasoning requires, a precise interpretation. The correct template is: we are C percent confident that the interval from (lower bound) to (upper bound) captures the true population proportion (described in context). Applying that template to the voter survey example from earlier chapters, where the 95 percent interval was 0.501 to 0.599, the correct interpretation is: we are 95 percent confident that the true proportion of all registered voters who support the ballot measure is between 50.1 percent and 59.9 percent.

What does '95 percent confident' mean underneath that sentence? It is a statement about the method, not about this particular interval. If you repeated the entire sampling process many times, drawing a new random sample of 400 voters each time and building a new confidence interval from each sample, approximately 95 percent of those intervals would end up containing the true population proportion p. The specific interval you calculated, 0.501 to 0.599, either does or does not contain the true p, there is no more randomness left once the data are collected and the interval is drawn. What is random is the interval's location before you draw the sample, not the fixed value of p. This is the same core idea introduced in general confidence interpretation, now applied to the specific case of a proportion.

Because of this subtlety, several common phrasings are technically wrong and worth naming explicitly so you can avoid them. Saying 'there is a 95 percent probability that the true proportion is in this interval' misstates a frequentist confidence interval as if p itself were random, when in fact p is a fixed, unknown constant and the interval's endpoints were the random part before sampling. Saying '95 percent of the data falls in this interval' confuses the goal, the interval is estimating a population parameter, not describing the spread of individual observations. Saying '95 percent of sample proportions will fall in this interval' is also incorrect, since only about 95 percent of the intervals built from different samples would capture p, not 95 percent of future p-hat values landing inside this one fixed interval.

The safest habit is to always interpret an interval using the full template: state the confidence level, name the interval's bounds, and describe the population parameter in the context of the problem. This keeps the langauge accurate and, just as importantly, keeps your understanding of what a confidence interval is actually doing accurate too.
